tile_description: Furnace runs but supply air is cool
quick_summary: Furnace lights but the supply air stays cool. Most callbacks on this complaint come from techs swapping whatever the board points at instead of proving what actually failed.

top_causes.cause: Weak or lost flame proving (lights, can't prove flame, drops out)
High-limit tripping from low airflow (overheats across the exchanger)
Draft, pressure switch, or condensate problems on 90+ units

diagnostic_steps.action: Watch one full sequence before touching anything
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Where the cycle fails (no ignition vs. light-and-drop vs. heats-then-cools) sends you to a different branch.

diagnostic_steps.action: If it lights and drops, meter flame current in series with the rod
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Most boards want 2-6 µA, brand-specific. Weak signal also means check ground, polarity, burner carryover — not just rod cleaning.

diagnostic_steps.action: Verify 24 VAC at the gas valve and manifold pressure (typically 3.5" WC NG)
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Voltage with no flow points downstream; erratic pressure points upstream to regulator or supply.

diagnostic_steps.action: If it heats then blows cold, measure temperature rise across the furnace
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Rise at or above plate top means airflow — check filter, coil, wheel, blower speed, zoning, static — not a bad limit.

diagnostic_steps.action: On a 90+ that stalls before ignition, prove draft with a manometer at the pressure-switch tap
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Should run at least 0.1" WC beyond switch close setpoint. Don't replace the switch until you've measured what it sees.

diagnostic_steps.action: Rollout open, or flame moves when blower starts? Stop and treat as combustion/HX
diagnostic_steps.rationale: These are safety events, not reset-and-walk events.

when_to_escalate: Stop and treat as combustion / heat exchanger problem if rollout is open or flame moves when the blower starts. Don't reset and leave.
field_warning: Don't swap pressure switches, high limits, or flame sensors without measuring first — that's the callback trap on this call.

quick_summary: Short cycling isn't one failure — it's a pattern. Identify the cycle type (burner-drop-with-blower-on, ignition-abort, control-side, or clean-cycles-no-faults) before touching anything.

top_causes.cause: Limit or airflow (burners run, drop with blower still on, restart)
Flame proving (burners light for seconds, drop, retry)
Pressure switch or draft on 90+ (inducer starts, aborts, retries)
Control-side / thermostat (W call disappears and comes back)
Oversizing (no faults, clean satisfactions, cycles under 5 minutes — not a repair)

diagnostic_steps.action: Time one full cycle with a stopwatch and pull active + stored fault codes
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Burner run length, off period, and code direction tell you which branch you're on before any parts swap.

diagnostic_steps.action: Meter R-W at the board through the cycle to confirm the W call is steady
diagnostic_steps.rationale: If W drops before satisfaction, the furnace is doing its job — problem is the stat, wiring, batteries, or cycle-rate setting. Honeywell recommends 3 CPH for 90%+.

diagnostic_steps.action: If burner drops with blower continuing, measure temperature rise and check static
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Classic limit cycle. Rise at/above plate top = airflow problem. Return static ≥0.4" WC is a red flag.

diagnostic_steps.action: If burner lights and drops in under a minute, meter flame current
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Brand-specific normal ranges. Weak signal means check ground, polarity, carryover, and gas pressure before condemning the rod.

diagnostic_steps.action: On 90+ ignition aborts, prove draft with a manometer (≥0.1" WC past switch close)
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Condensate backups masquerade as pressure-switch faults. Measure before swapping.

diagnostic_steps.action: No faults, normal numbers, cycles under 5 minutes? Call it oversizing
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Equipment-to-load mismatch. Not a parts call — needs a load calc and an honest conversation.

when_to_escalate: If the cycle is clean and short with no faults, don't part-swap — this is an oversizing or duct-design problem and needs a load calculation, not a repair.

tile_description: No ignition, no blower, nothing happening
quick_summary: Dead furnace call. Easy to skip steps and swap the wrong part. Walk the power path upstream methodically and most of these fall apart in about 10 minutes.

top_causes.cause: Line power or door interlock interrupted
Lost 24V — blown board fuse, failed transformer, or low-voltage short
Thermostat not delivering W (often smart stat with C-wire issue)
Open safety string — tripped float, stuck pressure switch, open limit/rollout

diagnostic_steps.action: Prove 120 VAC at the disconnect and at the board L1/neutral with door engaged
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Voltage loss between those points is the door interlock or internal wiring. Loose blower doors make a furnace look totally dead.

diagnostic_steps.action: Check transformer — 120 VAC primary, 24 VAC secondary
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Primary good with no secondary = transformer dead. Find what killed it (shorted accessory, T-stat wiring, float) before replacing.

diagnostic_steps.action: Inspect the board low-voltage fuse, then meter R-C for 24 VAC
diagnostic_steps.rationale: A blown fuse is a symptom of a short — find the short before the new fuse goes in.

diagnostic_steps.action: Meter W-C at the board during a heat call, then jumper R to W to bypass the stat
diagnostic_steps.rationale: If R-C is good but W-C is dead during the call, the problem is on the thermostat side. If the furnace runs jumpered, stop chasing furnace parts.

diagnostic_steps.action: Read the board code, then voltage-drop across each safety in the string
diagnostic_steps.rationale: 0 VAC across a closed switch, 24 VAC across the open one — fastest way to find the culprit without breaking connections.

diagnostic_steps.action: Check the condensate float and drain
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Float switches that break R kill the whole T-stat circuit and look like a dead stat. On some 90+ units the blocked-drain switch is in series with the gas valve.

diagnostic_steps.action: Only after all of the above, suspect the board
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Power, 24V, fuse, R-C, W call, and safeties all proven good — now a board call is justified, not a guess.

when_to_escalate: The board is the last suspect, not the first. Don't condemn it until line power, transformer, fuse, R-C, W-C, and the safety string are all proven good.
field_warning: A blown low-voltage fuse always means there's a short somewhere — drop a new fuse in without finding it and you'll blow the new one too.

tile_description: Water on the floor near the furnace
quick_summary: First question decides the call: 90%+ condensing furnace (which is supposed to make water and the leak is a drainage problem), or 80% standard furnace (which shouldn't be making water at all — water is usually tracking from above, or it's a venting problem).

top_causes.cause: 90%+ condensate path failure — clogged trap, blocked drain, wrong pitch, failed pump
On 80% units: water tracking down from AC coil above, humidifier, or plumbing — not the furnace at all
On 80% units: actual furnace water = venting or combustion problem (serious)
Heat exchanger or collector failure — only after drain path is fully ruled out

diagnostic_steps.action: Identify the furnace type — PVC + visible trap = 90%+, metal B-vent + no condensate = 80%
diagnostic_steps.rationale: This one-second ID changes everything that follows.

diagnostic_steps.action: Dry the area, run a heat call, and find the highest wet point with a flashlight and mirror
diagnostic_steps.rationale: If the top of the cabinet is wet before anything inside is, the source is above — coil, humidifier, plumbing, roof. Don't diagnose a furnace that isn't actually leaking.

diagnostic_steps.action: Check pitch — drain lines at 1/4" per foot toward drain, 90+ horizontal vent at 1/4" per foot back toward the furnace
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Sags, double traps, and bellies cause a lot of intermittent leaks.

diagnostic_steps.action: On 90%+, pull and flush the trap, inspect every port, verify orientation/height, prime before restart
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Partially clogged trap is the single most common 90+ leak — and it causes callbacks because it runs fine after reset until condensate backs up again.

diagnostic_steps.action: Clear the drain line downstream — flush, wet-vac, check for slime, sags, double traps, freeze risk on outdoor terminations
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Trap can be clean and the leak still comes back if the line downstream is blocked or routed wrong.

diagnostic_steps.action: Inspect the collector box, inducer housing, and internal drain paths for standing water or rust trails
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Standing water inside means condensate is backing up internally — points back to trap/drain/pitch, not 'replace the inducer.'

diagnostic_steps.action: If there's a condensate pump, fill the reservoir manually and watch float, discharge, and check valve under load
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Stuck float or bad check valve looks exactly like a furnace leak. Pump must be rated for acidic condensate.

diagnostic_steps.action: On 80% with confirmed furnace-source water, check venting and flue temp (~300-400°F healthy)
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Below 300°F suggests underfiring, oversized venting, or excessive heat extraction — condensation inside the vent corrodes the exchanger. Safety problem, not a drain problem.

when_to_escalate: If the trap is clean, drain is clear, pitch is right, vent is good, and water is still coming from inside the cabinet at a header or collector — you're past maintenance and into repair-or-replace with a safety conversation. On 80% units with confirmed furnace-source water, treat as a venting/combustion safety issue, not a drain problem.
field_warning: Water from an 80% furnace itself isn't a nuisance leak — it points to flue gas condensation, which corrodes the heat exchanger and is a combustion/CO concern.

tile_description: Blower runs, condenser hums, air is warm
quick_summary: AC is running but supply air is lukewarm. Most common mistake on this call is connecting gauges before checking anything else — airflow problems look like charge problems on a gauge set, and on A2L refrigerants every connection is handling risk. Non-invasive checks first.

top_causes.cause: Indoor airflow restriction — dirty filter, coil, blower wheel, or duct issue
Outdoor airflow or condenser problem — dirty coil, weak fan
Low refrigerant charge from an actual leak
Electrical (weak cap, pitted contactor, struggling compressor) and metering-device issues

diagnostic_steps.action: Measure return-to-supply temperature split (expect 16-22°F, broader 14-23°F by humidity)
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Free information. Low split = capacity loss; high split = low airflow. Frames everything that follows.

diagnostic_steps.action: Visual airflow triage — filter, evap face, blower wheel, flex, dampers, outdoor coil, condenser fan
diagnostic_steps.rationale: If the evap is iced, stop and thaw before any refrigerant diagnosis — frozen coils invalidate every reading.

diagnostic_steps.action: Pull total external static with a manometer before pulling gauges
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Field targets ~0.4-0.6" normal, 0.8"+ trouble, return ≥0.4" alone flags restriction. High TESP keeps you on airflow.

diagnostic_steps.action: Verify blower CFM and speed setup against the table (target 350-400 CFM/ton, ACCA QI within 15%)
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Low airflow explains most 'low on charge' misreads — low suction, freeze risk, high split.

diagnostic_steps.action: Inspect and clean indoor and outdoor coils, then recheck
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Dirty condenser drives high head and high-subcool patterns that look like overcharge. Dirty evap distorts SH and SC.

diagnostic_steps.action: Only now decide if gauges are warranted
diagnostic_steps.rationale: If airflow, static, coil cleanliness, and blower setup are all proven and split is still abnormal, connect. A2L systems especially reward this discipline.

diagnostic_steps.action: Charge by metering device — fixed orifice = target SH from chart; TXV = target SC from nameplate (~10°F ±3°F typical)
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Read the charging chart on the condenser. Pattern-read SH/SC together to separate undercharge, overcharge, low airflow, TXV restriction, non-condensables, and poor compression.

diagnostic_steps.action: Electrical checks — cap within ±6% of rated µF, contactor for pitting and voltage drop, compressor windings (C-R lowest, R-S = sum)
diagnostic_steps.rationale: Hard starting and bad compressor are different problems. Don't condemn a compressor before ruling out airflow, restrictions, and electrical support.

when_to_escalate: Compressor failure call is justified only after airflow, charge pattern, and electrical support parts are all proven. Before that, it's a guess. End-of-life conversation if compressor or coil failure on an older system — repair cost vs. age, reliability, and refrigerant type.
field_warning: On A2L systems (R-454B, R-32) every unnecessary connection is handling risk. Use A2L-rated recovery, vacuum, leak detector, and manifold — older A1 tools aren't acceptable. Lennox R-454B coils ship with factory leak-detection that can't mix with non-OEM sensors. Left-hand threaded hoses and a fire extinguisher on the truck.

tile_description: Boom, scrape, scream, or rumble from the unit
quick_summary: Most furnace sounds are benign — duct expansion, motor startup, normal ignition whoosh. A few are safety events. The whole job on this call is knowing the difference and being willing to shut equipment down when the noise is one of the dangerous ones.

shutdown_noises.what_it_means: Delayed ignition — gas accumulates then ignites all at once
shutdown_noises.action: Lock it out. Pull burners, inspect carryover slots, verify igniter position, manometer gas pressure, verify smooth light-off over multiple starts before returning to service.

shutdown_noises.noise: Burner roar or visible flame out the front
shutdown_noises.what_it_means: Flame rollout — combustion gases backing up out of the chamber
shutdown_noises.action: Shut down. Never jumper the rollout switch. Correct combustion air or venting before reset.

shutdown_noises.noise: Metal-on-metal scraping from the blower compartment
shutdown_noises.what_it_means: Wheel shifted on the shaft, broken mount, failed bearing, or foreign object
shutdown_noises.action: Shut down. Disconnect power before inspecting. Continued operation destroys the wheel, motor, and housing.

shutdown_noises.noise: Grinding or escalating bearing scream from the inducer
shutdown_noises.what_it_means: Inducer bearing failure — and the inducer is a combustion safety component, not just a fan
shutdown_noises.action: Shut down if escalating, severe, or paired with any pressure-switch trouble or rollout evidence.

shutdown_noises.noise: Combustion rumble or unstable roar from the burner section
shutdown_noises.what_it_means: Burner contamination, unstable flame, wrong gas pressure, venting issue, or combustion imbalance
shutdown_noises.action: Run combustion analysis. BPI: abort if ambient CO > 35 ppm; undiluted flue CO should stay under 100 ppm.

shutdown_noises.noise: Hissing or whistling that changes when the blower starts
shutdown_noises.what_it_means: Possible heat exchanger breach — flame disturbance on blower start is the AGA indicator
shutdown_noises.action: Shut down pending inspection. Watch flame before and during blower startup; displacement, floating, or rollout confirms the breach.

shutdown_noises.noise: Any of the above paired with a repeated safety trip
shutdown_noises.what_it_means: The safety is doing real work — the condition is unsafe
shutdown_noises.action: Lock out and find the cause. Never jumper a rollout. Don't reset and walk.

benign_noises: Smooth quick whoosh at ignition (normal light-off)
Duct expansion ticking and popping (sheet metal movement, not burner area)
Normal inducer startup ramp (light motor sound)
Mild cabinet resonance on blower startup (older transition pieces)
field_warning: Never jumper a rollout switch — not for a test, not for a customer, not ever. Don't reset repeated rollouts or ignition lockouts without finding the cause. Don't dismiss a noise because 'it's done that for months' — delayed ignition and rollout often persist right up until they cause real damage.
